guide.heading: Practical privacy and public-source guides
guide.description: Use focused workflows for account audits, research note protection, brand impersonation review and evidence logging.
guide.intro: Choose the task you need to finish. These guides provide action steps and worked examples; examples are labeled so they are not confused with observed research. The breach, password and account-security explainers below complement the public-source workflows.

sections.heading: Choose an outcome before collecting data
sections.body: For your own accounts, start with the digital-footprint checklist and username workflow. For a public-source report, use account-match verification and evidence logging. For a team, protect research notes before sharing screenshots, and use the brand-impersonation workflow when a lookalike makes a misleading claim. A larger collection of profile links is not a substitute for a verified account action or a supportable finding.

target.heading: Find public profiles: choose the right lookup method
target.description: Use specific GitHub, Instagram and Discord workflows, and distinguish exact handles, display names, login restrictions and unsupported checks.
target.intro: A platform lookup needs a method that fits the service. GitHub exposes a public user-search syntax. Instagram often limits signed-out access. Discord has no open web username directory, so MyRecon has no Discord username sweep and instead provides a separate numeric Discord ID lookup. Start with the guide for that workflow.

sections.heading: Other platforms: begin at the original service
sections.body:
If there is no detailed guide here, use the service's official search or an account link published by the owner, starting with the exact handle. A display name can return unrelated accounts, and search snippets can linger after a rename.

Do not guess undocumented URL patterns and read their HTTP status as a profile. A login page or challenge is an access limitation, and shop, organization, or forum accounts may need different interpretation from personal profiles.

sections.heading: Use a public sweep as a candidate list
sections.body: MyRecon's standard catalogue covers 560+ platforms, with guest previews and signed-in account allowances. Paid Extended scans have a separate catalogue. A catalogue entry does not guarantee a reliable response on every run. Open each found URL and keep unknown outcomes separate from not found. A username seen on another site does not prove common ownership, and not found does not establish registration availability.

sections.heading: Worked example: the same handle on two services
sections.body: Illustrative case: your saved signup email confirms an old forum account under example_handle, while an unrelated photo profile uses the same handle. The forum is a confirmed self-audit entry. The photo account remains unresolved. Retain the original URLs and the basis for each conclusion, then act only on the account you control. Avoid recovery probes or messages to the unrelated candidate.

sections.heading: A stopping rule saves unnecessary collection
sections.body: Stop when the required account has been confirmed or when no authorized source can answer the question. Write down an unavailable source rather than filling the gap with a guessed link. For account security, a saved login and official recovery process can matter more than a public scan. For a public association, an owner-published website link can be more useful than dozens of same-name results.

comparison.heading: Choose an OSINT workflow by task and evidence
comparison.description: Compare browser username checks, local command-line tools and breach lookups by input, access, output evidence and practical limits.
comparison.intro: The useful comparison is the question a tool can answer, the evidence it returns and the work needed to verify that evidence. A tool directory or the largest site count cannot settle whether a workflow meets your task. Start with the detailed Sherlock comparison, then use the decision criteria below.

sections.heading: Username discovery: browser or local command line
sections.body:
MyRecon offers a browser username workflow with free guest previews, five signed-in standard scans per day across 560+ platforms, and optional paid Extended packs. Sherlock and Maigret run locally from open-source repositories, while WhatsMyName was archived on 9 November 2026.

Prefer a local CLI when scripted integration and local output control matter, or browser access when installation is impractical. Both workflows require opening original sources and keeping unavailable checks separate.

sections.heading: Breach exposure is a different question
sections.body: Have I Been Pwned documents searches against its breach dataset. A breach entry can indicate exposure in that dataset; it does not prove that an account remains active, identify every service using an address or establish that a current password is compromised. A public username sweep cannot substitute for breach review. Choose the input and result type you need first, then follow the data source's response guidance.

sections.heading: Specialist tools and data providers
sections.body:
Graph tools, business-data APIs, and search aggregators have different inputs, data rights, and subscription terms, so do not assume they work like a username checker.

Check what each returned relationship actually means and whether it fits your authorized purpose. This hub does not claim to have tested every commercial provider; review official documentation and terms before purchasing or sharing identifiers.

sections.heading: A reproducible comparison sheet
sections.body:
Use an account or identifier you control and record the version, date, input, scan scope, positive and negative controls, returned URLs, unavailable checks, and manually verified outcomes.

Separate setup effort from request duration. An HTTP 200 status is not proof of a profile, a random string is not a verified negative control, and blocked checks belong in the denominator as unavailable.

sections.heading: Worked decision and published limits
sections.body:
Illustrative task: find and close your own old accounts from two remembered usernames. A browser sweep plus saved signup emails is usually enough without the setup overhead of a graph platform, while repeatable local exports favor a CLI.

The homepage includes a recorded MyRecon username case with captured evidence, though its small scope is not a general accuracy score or a same-scope benchmark of every tool named here.

deletion.heading: Remove or reduce your public information
deletion.description: Separate account deletion, broker opt-outs and search-result removal. Prepare exports, use official channels and verify each request outcome.
deletion.intro: There are three different actions: delete an account you control, suppress a broker listing, or remove a search result pointing to a source page. Each has a different owner and verification step. Use this decision guide to avoid submitting the wrong request or losing access to data you wanted to keep.

sections.heading: 1. Decide who controls the source
sections.body:
Open the original page and record its exact URL, date, and the fields you want removed. For your own social account, use provider settings; for a broker listing, submit that broker's privacy request; for stale snippets after removal, use the search engine's refresh tool.

Removing a Google result does not delete the original page. Where the source belongs to another person or organization, contact its owner or the official reporting channel.

sections.heading: 2. Prepare account deletion before confirming it
sections.body:
Sign in through the official app or website, export data you want to keep, transfer shared repositories or workspaces, and update other accounts that use this login for sign-in or recovery.

Cancel active subscriptions in their own billing channel because deleting a profile may not stop app-store billing. Check the provider's deactivation-versus-deletion rules and waiting period before confirming.

sections.heading: 3. Submit a broker request using the exact record
sections.body:
Locate your matching record before entering an opt-out flow, and submit the request through the broker's official privacy channel using a verification email you control.

Share only required fields and check redaction options if ID is requested; MyRecon does not collect documents or submit requests for you. Save the reference number and remember that broker suppression rarely removes upstream public records.

sections.heading: 4. Use Google removal for the correct condition
sections.body:
Google separates removing personal information on a live page from refreshing an outdated snippet after a source page has already changed. Choose the route that matches the current page and provide both exact URLs.

Save the decision rather than treating submission as removal. A delisted result can still stay reachable directly or through another search engine.

sections.heading: 5. Verify each outcome and record what remains
sections.body:
After the provider's stated processing period, reopen the exact original URL in a signed-out window, inspect the search result separately, and record removed, changed, still visible, or unable to verify.

Never treat an acknowledgement email as proof of removal. Recheck broker pages after a refresh cycle because listings can reappear, and delete redundant screenshots once follow-up ends.

sections.heading: Worked example: address on a broker page
sections.body:
Illustrative case: a broker page displays your old home address and Google indexes that URL. First request suppression at the broker and save its case number, then request an outdated-content refresh from Google once the broker page disappears.

Record those as two separate outcomes. If the source stays live, use Google's personal-information removal criteria instead; no single request clears every archive or public record.
